article.articleHeadline: Rapid progression of Japanese encephalitis: a child in a coma and respiratory failure after several days of fever.
article.articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis (JE) can start with fever and headache and rapidly progress to altered consciousness, seizures, coma, and respiratory failure in children, with no specific antiviral therapy. At Vietnam’s National Hospital for Tropical Diseases, several pediatric JE cases were treated, including a 9-year-old from Lao Cai who deteriorated from fever to coma within days, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. After two weeks of intensive care, consciousness improved, and the child could breathe independently, though weakness and impaired coughing persisted, with ongoing risk of neuro-sequelae. About 50% of JE survivors develop long-term neurodevelopmental, motor, or behavioral issues. JE is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes; there is no human-to-human transmission. In Hanoi, June 2026 marked the year's first JE case, while 2025 had none. Vaccination is essential: three primary doses plus boosters every 3–4 years up to age 15. Emphasize mosquito bite prevention and environmental control.

article.articleHeadline: Expand Specialized Laboratories to Respond to Infectious Diseases.
article.articleSummary: On August 18, 2026, the Pasteur Institute in Ho Chi Minh City activated its Advanced Diagnostic Unit (ADU), expanding specialized laboratory capacity to detect, diagnose, surveil, and respond to emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases in southern Vietnam and nationwide. The unit responds to decades of regional exposure to new pathogens, with milestones including HIV first detected in Vietnam (1990), avian influenza (2003), the first COVID-19 cases in Ho Chi Minh City (early 2020), and mpox first reported in Vietnam (2022). Initiated in 2023 with domestic and international experts, the ADU is supported by the Association of Public Health Laboratories (APHL). It is equipped for integrated molecular biology and diagnostics, featuring PCR platforms, multiplex immunoassay systems, and next-generation sequencing, aligning with national public health surveillance and response efforts.

article.articleHeadline: Man not bitten by a tick but in critical condition due to a tick-borne disease; condition deteriorates rapidly after tending the vegetable garden.
article.articleSummary: In Zhejiang Province, a 57-year-old man (Wang Dabo) developed high fever and chills after working in his home vegetable garden. He was admitted to Zhejiang Provincial People’s Hospital Infectious Diseases Department; labs showed severe leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and dysfunction of coagulation and liver tests. Combined with external hospital serology/NA tests, he was diagnosed with a novel bunyavirus infection, i.e., Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS), a tick-borne disease. He had no obvious tick bite mark; clinicians suspect environmental exposure as the virus can enter via micro-skin cuts. SFTS can progress rapidly, triggering systemic inflammation and potential multi-organ failure. After about one week of treatment, his platelet count rose and liver function improved, and he was discharged. Dr. Yang Danhong warns that infection can occur without tick bites; preventive measures include wearing protective clothing, using repellents, and checking exposed areas after outdoor activity. Seek care within 1–2 weeks of fever or fatigue and report exposure history.

article.articleHeadline: Multiple respiratory viruses co-circulating; doctors offer tips on timely testing for high-risk groups.
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 positivity rate declined in week 32 surveillance (Aug 3–9, 2026) in China, with overall moderate circulation. High-risk groups—older adults, young children, pregnant women, and those with underlying diseases or severe obesity—should seek early medical evaluation and testing if fever with cough occurs; testing is advised when multiple household members present with flu-like symptoms or after known exposure. Some provincial hospitals offer 24/7 nucleic acid testing; labs can multiplex seven pathogens (COVID-19, influenza A/B, rhinovirus, adenovirus, RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae) to guide treatment. In Changsha, offline pharmacies report ample COVID-19 and flu antigen tests; PCR remains more sensitive, while antigen tests enable rapid home screening but may yield false negatives."

Authorities urge vaccination for high-risk groups and advise the public to avoid close contact with suspected infections.

article.articleHeadline: Quanzhou City hosts the 2026 Tuberculosis Prevention and Control Skills Competition.
article.articleSummary: On August 18, 2026, Quanzhou City hosted the 2026 Tuberculosis Prevention and Control Skills Competition, organized by the Quanzhou Health Commission and General Trade Union, and hosted by Quanzhou Center for Disease Control and Prevention. Fifty-two TB professionals from CDCs, TB-designated hospitals, and grassroots clinics competed to test TB control knowledge and skills. The contest covered theory, skills, and teamwork, assessing the TB control spectrum from fundamentals to outbreak response, lab standards, and clinical management. After two days, awards included six team prizes, three outstanding-organization prizes, plus one Special Contribution Award and one Outstanding Personal Award; six individuals in each of the Prevention & Control and Clinical Diagnosis & Treatment tracks. Track winners may be nominated for the provincial competition for the Quanzhou Gold Medal Worker title. The event aims to standardize procedures and strengthen capacity for early TB detection, reporting, diagnosis, treatment, management, and screening with patient-centered care.

article.articleHeadline: Summer Water Fun: Beware of Infection by This Parasite
article.articleSummary: Pathogenic free-living amoebae—Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba, and Balamuthia mandrillaris—are environmental in fresh water, sediment, soil, and dust. In China, infections are extremely rare; no human-to-human transmission or cluster outbreaks. Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAME) after nasal exposure to contaminated water; incubation 1–7 days; early fever and severe headache rapidly progress to seizures, neck stiffness, coma; mortality exceeds 96%, with a very narrow treatment window. Acanthamoeba causes keratitis (notably in contact lens wearers), skin infections, and granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE) in immunocompromised, often subacute to chronic. Balamuthia mandrillaris can cause indolent skin lesions that later invade the CNS (GAE); mortality over 90%. Preventive measures: swim in licensed facilities, avoid still or muddy waters, do not use tap water for lens cleaning, disinfect wounds, and seek immediate care if high fever and neurological symptoms follow water exposure.

article.articleHeadline: On This Day | Hong Kong scrambles to contain cholera outbreak in 1961 - SCMP archive
article.articleSummary: Four cholera cases confirmed in Hong Kong on August 17, 1961, prompting declaration of the Colony as an infected area. Two deaths were reported, and another suspected case was admitted to Lai Chi Kok Hospital. In response, vaccination centers were opened and mobile health inspectors, with police, were deployed to inspect street markets for cut fruit and other dangerous goods; offending stocks would be confiscated. Two special committees were established to coordinate the response, including one under the Director of Medical and Health Services that would meet daily to organize health and medical activities during the cholera threat. The measures illustrate a rapid containment effort aimed at curbing spread of cholera in Hong Kong.

article.articleHeadline: Warning from an expert: no one monitors experiments with dangerous viruses that could spark the next pandemic.
article.articleSummary: Warning: no universal monitoring of experiments with dangerous viruses that could spark the next pandemic. A Cell study (Feb) by Chinese virologists analyzed nearly 1,000 bat samples from five provinces stored at the Wuhan Institute of Virology to find coronaviruses near human infection. Some samples carried relatives of MERS; researchers showed one virus could enter human cells via the same cell receptor used by the viruses that cause SARS and Covid-19. The virus was cultured in lab-adapted human airway and gut cells and proposed for testing in mice engineered with the human receptor. Although features limiting human infection were identified, further work could remove barriers. Conducted outside high containment, prompting alarms that safety levels were inadequate for airborne spillover. The piece calls for binding global standards, currently lacking. Fort Detrick incident in Maryland shows security failures; 53 BSL-4 labs operate in 22 countries, with about 300 lab infections reported 2000–2021; SARS-like viruses have escaped from high-containment facilities.

article.articleSummary: On 18 August 2026, Tanum, Sweden reported a high-pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 outbreak. The Centre has notified Swedish authorities and will continue to monitor updates from the World Organisation for Animal Health and relevant authorities, taking appropriate action as local outbreak developments evolve.

article.articleHeadline: 'Swill feeding pigs' officially included in the ban, cutting off the transmission chain of African swine fever.
article.articleSummary: China’s Ecological Environment Code, effective August 15, 2026, formally bans feeding pigs with unanalyzed kitchen waste (swill), upgrading a 2018 State Council notification to law. The measure targets African swine fever (ASF) transmission: ASF has near-100% mortality, no vaccine, and a virus that survives for years at low temperatures and weeks at room temperature; heating to 70°C for 30 minutes is required to inactivate it. Global tracing of 219 ASF outbreaks from 2008–2012 found nearly half were linked to swill feeding. In China, 2018 saw 21 ASF outbreaks, with about 62% related to swill feeding. The outbreak wave caused extensive culling, slashed production, and soaring pork prices, highlighting the risk of feed-savings against massive disease losses. The ban aims to cut the swill transmission chain and stabilize the pork supply.

article.articleHeadline: Lesotho Readies Botswana-Made FMD Vaccines as Key Wool and Mohair Industry Faces Restrictions
article.articleSummary: Lesotho reports its first confirmed foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) outbreak, with vaccination to begin after receiving 100,000 doses from Botswana on Aug 17, 2026. Botswana pledged the vaccine and veterinary training during the June 18 Lesotho-Botswana Bi-National Commission in Gaborone. The outbreak started in February in Butha-Buthe; 17 cattle were sampled, with 6 testing positive for FMD antibodies by a non-structural protein ELISA. Quarantine, movement restrictions, and intensified surveillance are in effect. The wool and mohair sector—about 2 million sheep and roughly M900 million annually—accounts for ~60% of agricultural exports. China briefly restricted imports, later lifting after negotiations and new sanitary requirements. A July 3 protocol requires heat-treatment of untreated wool/mohair from FMD areas; Lesotho uses 37°C for eight days, with facilities approved, and Botswana veterinary specialists to train local personnel before vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola-related mortality declines at the Kigonze site in Ituri.
article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease mortality is declining at the Kigonze IDP site in Bunia, Ituri province. Authorities report 1–3 deaths per day among an estimated 17,000 residents, down from a peak of eight daily in June–July. Improved community adherence to prevention measures and reduced high-risk practices, such as direct handling of patients or bodies, contribute to the improvement. A parallel decrease in positive cases is observed in Nyakunde health zone. Response teams have strengthened epidemiological surveillance and directed suspected cases to treatment centers in the Nizi health zone. Ongoing challenges include a potable-water shortage hindering handwashing and hygiene, with persistent resistance to health directives in Nizi. Coordination urges sustaining gains, boosting water supply at displacement sites, and preventing a new outbreak surge in densely populated areas.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Bunia: the fear of contamination is driving down the.
article.articleSummary: On 18 August 2026, Ebola resurgence in Bunia, Ituri Province, DR Congo, is driving fear of contamination and reducing health-seeking behavior. Attendance at the AERO Health Center has fallen about 80%, from around 200 patients per day pre-epidemic to roughly 40 today. Health workers have intensified triage and prevention measures. The center's lead nurse, Chantal Buregeya, notes that patients are screened for Ebola case-defining symptoms like fever, headache, and abdominal pain; those with signs are separated and directed to an isolation room outside the main building. Clinicians stress that prevention and isolation protocols exist to limit transmission, and urge residents not to forgo care due to fear, to seek care promptly for symptoms, enabling early referral to specialized facilities and reducing complications and spread. Response actors call Bunia residents to maintain health service use while observing preventive measures.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola outbreak: how to stop the spread of the virus across
article.articleSummary: Outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, declared May 15, 2026, has become the deadliest in the country. As of August 18, 2026, 4,945 laboratory-confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths have been reported, surpassing the 2018–2020 epidemic (2,299 deaths). The outbreak spans six provinces, driven by Ebola virus species Bundibugyo, for which there is no licensed vaccine or approved specific treatment; research and trials are ongoing. The article examines why the spread is accelerating, the adequacy of the response, and measures to halt inter-provincial transmission. It features a discussion with Dr. Anicet Kipasa, a public health expert and former vice-president of the Ebola International Scientific and Technical Committee in Kikwit, chaired by Prof. Jean-Jacques Muyembe-Tamfum. The focus is on breaking transmission chains and mobilizing authorities, health workers, and communities.

article.articleHeadline: That will be the mother of all Ebola outbreaks in Africa.
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) risks becoming Africa's deadliest. Airports near the DRC implement screening via questionnaires, travel history, seat data, QR codes, and temperature checks. First infections may date to February; outbreak identified in May. In the three months since, >2,300 died and ~4,600 infected, the worst Ebola epidemic in the DRC to date. The eastern region, a war zone, suffers weak contact tracing and scarce lab staff. Manenji Mangundu called it 'the mother of all Ebola outbreaks in Africa.' Funding shortfalls hinder response: 2024 US humanitarian aid ~$881M and health aid ~$387M; 2025 humanitarian ~$126M (-85%) and health ~$279M (-28%); 2026 funding projected at ~$732M. No approved vaccines or therapies exist for Bundibugyo ebolavirus; Ervebo may offer partial protection. Attacks on health workers and Ebola denial complicate control; education campaigns must restart, per Muyembe-Tamfum.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola is back, but the IMF's emergency relief fund is running dry
article.articleSummary: Ebola returns to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with more than 2,000 deaths confirmed; UNDP warns outbreak could push nearly 1 million people into poverty. The Congo crisis exposes a gap between rapid health response needs and slow mobilization of finance. IMF's Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust (CCRT) has about $120 million available, but Congo faces almost $300 million in IMF debt service in 2027, underscoring funding gaps. Proposals: monetize part of IMF gold reserves—roughly 90.5 million troy ounces held, historically valued at $45/oz but trading near $4,000/oz—selling ~10% could raise tens of billions; a $35.8 billion endowment yielding ~3% could provide >$1 billion annually for concessional financing and debt relief, reducing dependence on repeated donor campaigns. Any sale requires 85% IMF members; US leadership is pivotal to act.

article.articleHeadline: In Tucumán, influenza and bronchiolitis notifications remain stable.
article.articleSummary: Argentina’s Tucumán province convened a new Epidemiological Situation Room led by Health Minister Luis Medina Ruiz to review international, national, and provincial health trends, focusing on vaccine-preventable diseases, arboviruses, and respiratory infections. International alerts include measles in Guatemala, Mexico, Peru, and the United States; travelers should complete the National Vaccination Calendar before visiting affected areas. Global Ebola activity is noted in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda. Nationally, a dengue case in Buenos Aires City is under investigation, and chikungunya totals reach 3,618 with no new cases since epidemiological week 29 of 2026. Tucumán reports no recent dengue or chikungunya. Respiratory trends show an early 2026 rise in Influenza A (H3N2 and related subtypes) with a later shift to Influenza B; locally influenza and bronchiolitis remain stable, with rhinovirus and RSV cocirculation and bronchiolitis declining. Preventive measures emphasize ventilation and electrical safety during cold weather.

article.articleSummary: Ebola virus disease response sensitization for state agents in Haut-Uélé, North-East Democratic Republic of Congo, took place in Isiro on August 18, 2026. Vice-Governor Christophe Dara urged authorities to mobilize the population to adopt barrier measures and hygienic practices to curb transmission and protect families. He noted that the province currently faces an Ebola outbreak across more than six of its thirteen health zones, with about 140 confirmed or suspected cases and an estimated case fatality rate of around 80%. The official warned that, if the population adheres to preventive behavior, no Ebola cases could remain in Haut-Uélé within 21 days. The training occurred at the governors’ official residence in Isiro, underscoring prevention and rapid response as critical to stopping spread and ensuring community ownership of hygiene and protection measures.

article.articleHeadline: Rabies-infected youth who fled after breaking into a hospital and lay on the road died three months later due to not getting ARV - Baghpat: man dies of rabies 3 months after dog bite, no ARV.
article.articleSummary: Rabies fatality in Baghpat district, Uttar Pradesh: A 35-year-old man, Anis Ansari of Laliana, was bitten by a stray dog about three months earlier and did not receive Anti-Rabies Vaccine (ARV). Rabies was confirmed at Anand Hospital in Meerut; he was referred to Delhi, but GTB Hospital in Shahdara reportedly declined treatment. His family moved him between Delhi and UP facilities, and he died en route to a hospital in Gajraula. He had already shown rabies symptoms and was later admitted to Shri Maharishi Valmiki Hospital in Bawana, Delhi, where he was reportedly kept in a room and died on the road. He is survived by a son and a daughter. Health officials urge ARV for all household contacts after dog bites, advise washing the wound with soap and water for 10–15 minutes, warn against home remedies, and emphasize prompt ARV and tetanus vaccination.

article.articleHeadline: During the monsoon season, cows and buffaloes are at risk of foot-and-mouth disease, with lesions in the mouth and hooves—here's how to prevent it.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) poses a high risk to cows and buffaloes in Eastern Champaran, India, during the monsoon. In Harsidi block, farmer Rajiv Ranjan warns that FMD causes painful lesions in the mouth, tongue, gums, and hooves, with fever and reduced milk production; calves can be severely affected, sometimes dying. Infected animals should be isolated immediately to prevent spread. Vaccination is crucial; animals should be vaccinated before the rains, and farmers should participate in government vaccination campaigns. If vaccination isn’t available locally, contact the block veterinary officer for options. There is no immediate cure; emphasis is on prevention, including keeping shelters clean and dry, providing clean water and nutritious feed, and seeking veterinary advice promptly when symptoms appear during the monsoon period.

article.articleHeadline: A dose of insecticide killed 97.91% of mosquitoes that spread dengue; a tiny fraction that survived has researchers in Delhi worried
article.articleSummary: University of Delhi researchers in India report that a laboratory Aedes aegypti strain, the dengue vector, showed 97.91% mortality at the WHO diagnostic dose of α-cypermethrin (10 µg per bottle) in bottle bioassay, slightly below the 98% threshold for susceptibility. In tests with 12 concentrations, four replicates and 20 female mosquitoes per bottle, mortality was recorded at 24 hours. Lakhwani warns this could signal emerging resistance, though survivors were not shown to transmit reduced susceptibility. Biochemical analysis indicated a detoxification enzyme response: β-esterase showed strongest binding to α-cypermethrin, up to ~21-fold at LC50 and ~17-fold at LC90; CYP450 ~2x; α-esterase >7x; glutathione S-transferase declined and acetylcholinesterase showed weak binding. The insecticide targets voltage-gated sodium channels; repeated use may select for resistance traits. Aedes aegypti transmits dengue and spreads Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever. WHO estimates large dengue burden; recommendations include insecticide rotations, biological controls, and household measures to remove breeding sites.

article.articleHeadline: Leptospirosis makes its entry in Patna; second woman to test positive at NMCH in five days; how does this disease spread?
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis detected in Patna, Bihar, with Nalanda Medical College Hospital (NMCH) as the state’s sole public facility for testing. In NMCH’s microbiology department, four suspected samples were examined; a 31-year-old woman from Khushrupur tested positive for Leptospira IgM. This marks the second female case within five days; previously, on Aug 13, a 48-year-old woman from Agamkuan also tested IgM-positive in the same lab. NMCH has been designated a surveillance center and provides free testing for government patients; testing at other government hospitals is routed to NMCH. Transmission occurs via contact with the urine of wild rats, contaminated water, or soil, with flood season increasing rat movement into populated areas and elevating risk. The patient is stable and receiving treatment; awareness programs will be organized by the Medicine Department.

article.articleHeadline: Lumpy Skin Disease: In Uttar Pradesh, 12 districts affected by LSD; one more in Kanpur and 6,514 cattle infected in Hapur.
article.articleSummary: Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) has spread from Haryana to Uttar Pradesh, with cases now in Kanpur Nagar and Hapur. In Hapur, 51 cattle are infected (23 recovered); in Kanpur Nagar’s Kalyanpur, 1 infection confirmed. Across 12 districts, LSD has infected 6,514 cattle, with 5,332 recovered and 1,182 under treatment; no cattle deaths have been reported. Previously affected districts include Amroha, Bagpat, Bijnor, Firozabad, Ghaziabad, Mathura, Meerut, Muzaffarnagar, Saharanpur, and Shamli. Response includes quarantine, treatment, vaccination, and samples sent for testing, plus ring vaccination within a 5 km radius around infected zones. Cumulative LSD vaccination exceeds 648,689 cattle in the state. Authorities continue continuous monitoring and have issued updated guidelines for all affected districts.

article.articleHeadline: Malajkhund Copper Project Is Increasing Disease in Tribal Villages.
article.articleSummary: Malajkhund copper project in Balaghat district’s Bahar and Birsa blocks is linked to rising skin and infectious diseases and child deaths in tribal villages, notably Borhekada and Chhinditola. Contaminated, chemically polluted water from the plant has severely affected households, with widespread skin ailments, severe infections, and respiratory issues such as asthma and coughing. The toxic effluent has devastated crops and livelihoods, threatening farming and local ecology, and wildlife deaths have been reported. Although HCL reportedly adopted the villages, residents say development remains distant and health camps dispense only routine medicines. MP Bharti Paradhi visited, urging improvements, but no concrete action followed. Residents demand scientific testing of water, soil, and crops, accountability, and provision of clean drinking water and relief to affected families.

article.articleHeadline: Vizag man diagnosed with rare disease after 6 years of suspected TB
article.articleSummary: Visakhapatnam, India—A 32-year-old man with six years of recurrent lymph node swelling was ultimately diagnosed with Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (KFD), a rare inflammatory lymphadenitis that can mimic tuberculosis or lymphoma. He first developed fever with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy and leukopenia in 2020; biopsy showed granulomatous changes and anti-tuberculosis therapy was started, though fever persisted after four weeks and oral ulcers plus blood abnormalities appeared. Repeated microbiological tests for TB were negative, prompting reassessment. In 2022 he again presented with swelling and was treated as TB. Recently at KIMS Hospitals, Seethammadhara, he had painful swelling in the right axilla. A comprehensive evaluation integrating histopathology, microbiology, immunology and clinical findings established Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease. He completed treatment and was discharged stable. The case underscores not to assume TB or lymphoma in recurrent lymphadenopathy and to interpret granulomatous changes in a multidisciplinary context.

article.articleHeadline: Connecting Care: Community-based Model Transforming TB And HIV Services
article.articleSummary: TB remains the leading cause of death among people living with HIV, with over 150,000 HIV-TB deaths in 2024 and 570,000 AIDS-related deaths in 2025. In India, HPPI advocates integrating TB services into existing HIV care platforms (ART centres) via the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) and National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) to identify TB earlier and improve treatment completion. Since Dec 7, 2024, NTEP deployed AI-enabled handheld X-ray TB screening plus upfront rapid molecular testing, including mobile vans reaching high-risk communities, identifying over a million asymptomatic TB cases in a year. Between May and July 2026, HPPI screened 1,363 people living with HIV using a ten-symptom verbal screen plus chest X-ray; 259 were presumptive TB, 21 diagnosed, with 12 (57%) of them asymptomatic. The approach highlights screening at every HIV visit and leveraging community networks to reduce transmission and deaths.

A ₹5.90-crore sewage diversion pipeline is sanctioned to prevent sewage entry, and the Priyadarshini Park sewage treatment plant upgrade to 10 million litres per day is underway; the diversion pipeline will connect to the STP to provide a long-term solution.

article.articleHeadline: Climate Change Could Redraw the Malaria Map in Sub-Saharan Africa, Research Finds
article.articleSummary: Climate change is expected to redraw sub-Saharan Africa's childhood malaria map, increasing risk in cooler highlands of East and southern Africa while reducing transmission in some hottest regions. By 2050 and 2100, mosquitoes carrying malaria could invade cooler Ethiopian and Kenyan highlands, Angola, Zambia, and northeastern South Africa, with coastal southern Africa potentially seeing up to a 20% rise by 2100. Conversely, parts of West and Central Africa (Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali) could see transmission fall as temperatures exceed optimal ranges. The paper notes transmission peaks near 25 C and declines below 16 C or above 34 C; heavy rainfall followed by 2–3 months later correlates with higher prevalence. In Africa, malaria deaths were about 579,000 in 2024, ~75% among children under 5. Limiting warming to 2 C could avert about five additional childhood malaria cases per 1,000 children in southern Africa; stronger malaria surveillance and control are needed.

article.articleHeadline: North Korea bans entry of visitors from 12 African countries amid concerns about the spread of Ebola... France excluded.
article.articleSummary: North Korea tightened Ebola-related border controls by barring visa issuance and entry for foreigners who have traveled to 12 African countries since May 2026, effective Aug 14, 2026. The countries are the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya, Zambia, Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Republic of Congo, and Burundi. Affected individuals cannot obtain visas or enter North Korea, per Vostok Intur, cited by Radio Free Asia (RFA). France was initially included but was removed last week after North Korea’s partner said France is no longer considered to be in an Ebola-transmission zone. WHO declared a public health emergency for Ebola on May 16, and Russia reportedly provided Bundibugyo Ebola diagnostic kits to North Korea in June. Historically, North Korea sealed borders during the 2014 West Africa Ebola outbreak, imposing a 3‑week quarantine for some entrants for about four months.

The incidence in Bashkortostan was 0.05 per 100,000, about half the Russian average (0.12 per 100,000, 178 cases) and 24.7% below the Volga Federal District rate (0.07 per 100,000, 19 cases). In 2024, Bashkortostan reported 5 dengue cases (0.12 per 100,000) and in 2023, 3 cases (0.07 per 100,000). Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions; travelers to endemic regions (Thailand, UAE, and other Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern destinations) should use repellents, wear long clothing, and sleep under mosquito nets.

article.articleHeadline: Antibody dynamics after melioidosis infection in Thailand: a retrospective cohort study
article.articleSummary: Melioidosis infection in Thailand analyzed for antibody dynamics in a retrospective cohort. The study tracks longitudinal humoral responses after infection to elucidate how antibody levels change over time. Conducted by a multinational team spanning Mahidol University (Bangkok), Mahidol-Oxford Tropical Medicine Research Unit, Cambodia Oxford Medical Research Unit, and partners in the United States (UC Davis; University of Nevada, Reno; University of Washington) and the United Kingdom (University of Oxford; London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine), the work draws on Thai patient data to map antibody trajectories post-melioidosis. The article emphasizes antibody dynamics and their potential implications for understanding immunity and surveillance in endemic Southeast Asia. Published 2026-08-18.

article.articleHeadline: Catch Your Breath: Follow Your Child's Breath - An awareness-raising campaign to help parents understand RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) in children
article.articleSummary: Thailand's Ogilvy and MSD launch Catch Your Breath: Follow Your Child's Breath to raise awareness of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in children. The campaign reframes RSV from a routine seasonal alert into an experiential understanding for parents, noting that about 9 in 10 children are infected with RSV before age two. It emphasizes that RSV is not just a cold; laboratory insight shows pediatric RSV can push breathing rates above 60 breaths per minute. A short film has three RSV-affected families run on a treadmill; once pace rises, parents' breathing hits 35 breaths per minute, about half of what their infants endure during RSV. The Little Marathoners billboard and Thai wordplay on 'Catch Your Breath' aim to make parents aware that infants' lungs cannot sustain maximal air intake for days. RSV season runs July–November; the campaign urges protection and medical consultation. Video at YouTube link.

article.articleHeadline: Explainer: A severe drought has brought back the deadly disease to Brazil; after 73 years, how did 'Yellow Fever' return to the cities?
article.articleSummary: Yellow fever re-emerged in Brazilian cities between 2016 and 2019 after the disease had been declared eliminated in 1942. About 2,000 people were infected and around 750 died, prompting surprise among health authorities. Stanford and Princeton researchers, reporting in Science Advances, traced the outbreak to the century's worst drought in 2015, driven by El Niño, which dried forest water sources in Brazil and across South America. Water and food scarcity forced howler and marmoset monkeys toward urban areas, many carrying the virus. Haemagogus mosquitoes, stressed by drought, increased biting and accompanied the primates into settlements, enabling human infections. Mass vaccination and vector-control measures eventually halted the outbreak. The work highlights that climate-driven shifts in wildlife behavior can introduce zoonoses into cities, raising concern that future droughts could trigger similar outbreaks in Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Noeul secures Health Canada Class II medical device license for "Malaria Diagnostic Cartridge."
article.articleSummary: Malaria diagnostic cartridge miLab MAL Cartridge received Health Canada Class II medical device license on August 18, 2026. Noeul, an AI-based blood and cancer diagnostics company, reports that the miLab MAL cartridge is the core component of its AI malaria diagnostic solution and that approval enables continued review of the miLab platform license, with final steps underway. Upon platform licensure, the company plans local commercialization in Canada, including discussions with distributors to supply hospitals and testing laboratories and to establish market entry pathways. The miLab MAL solution uses on-device AI and solid-state staining technology to automate the full microscopy workflow—from sample prep and imaging to AI analysis—with results in under 15 minutes. Noeul previously earned MDSAP certification in five countries, including Canada, the United States, and Brazil, paving a path for broader overseas expansion. The company intends to leverage these regulatory experiences for other markets.

article.articleHeadline: Imported from Rio de Janeiro, how did dengue spread throughout Ceará?
article.articleSummary: Dengue arrived in Ceará in 1986, imported from Nova Iguaçu, Rio de Janeiro, amid a tourism-driven surge. The first DENV-1 cases appeared in Aracati and later Fortaleza, linked to travelers returning from Rio during an epidemic. The outbreak unfolded as Aedes aegypti, long present in Ceará, enabled sustained transmission; vector reintroductions had been detected in 1984 (Aquiraz) and reinfestation in Fortaleza, with larvae found near BR-116, Mercado São Sebastião, Rodoviário, Port, and Airport. By August 1986, infestation indices in Fortaleza exceeded 30%, and 20 Ceará municipalities were infested, prompting urgent control measures. The Ministry of Health labeled the situation grave. The initial May 1986 case of Ilza Santos do Nascimento was suspected for dengue but later downgraded due to lack of local serology, illustrating early diagnostic uncertainty. Researchers highlight the vector's adaptability and the health system's limited early responsiveness.

article.articleHeadline: Senepa begins installation of "ovitraps" in seven critical neighborhoods of Ciudad del Este - Diario Vanguardia
article.articleSummary: Malaria control authorities in Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, begin deploying ovitraps to locate mosquito breeding hotspots. The National Malaria Eradication Service (Senepa) will install about 25 ovitraps per stratum across seven neighborhoods that registered the most cases in previous years. The pots contain a paddle with an attractant that lures mosquitoes to lay eggs; samples collected are sent to the laboratory to assess larval infestation and identify zones with the highest mosquito activity. Results will guide rapid interventions—chemical and physical controls and space spraying. Installations start this week and traps will remain in place for several days before collection. Officials warn of forecast heavy, continuous rains due to El Niño, which can boost mosquito populations, prompting active cross-border coordination with Itaipú Binacional and Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: In a twist, the MPF defends the slaughter of llamas seized in Acre due to risk of foot-and-mouth disease.

The shift follows new technical data from the Ministry of Agriculture showing the animals lack documentation of origin, health history, or legal entry, leaving transmission risk unresolved. Although an IDAF inspection found no clinical signs, camelids are susceptible to FMD, and unregulated entry could jeopardize Brazil's FMD-free status without vaccination, with major implications for agriculture and trade. Quarantine, return, or re-export were rejected due to lack of traceability and absence of isolated quarantine facilities in the state. The animals were seized on May 20 at a BR-364 inspection post and are under the NGO Patinha Carente in Porto Acre; 13 have died (10 at the shelter), with a Federal Court decision pending in Rio Branco.

article.articleHeadline: Peru records a worrying 41% increase in dengue cases in 2026: 42,000 cases and 48 deaths.
article.articleSummary: Dengue cases in Peru rose 41% in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 42,440 infections through epidemiological week 31 (by August 8) with 48 deaths nationwide. La Libertad recorded the sharpest rise, from 2025’s 202 cases to 5,677 in 2026. Piura followed with 7,641 cases (up from 980), and Lambayeque with 3,667 (from 648). Madre de Dios increased from 218 to 1,808; Ucayali from 362 to 2,826. San Martín has the most fatalities (12), followed by Lambayeque (10) and Madre de Dios (8); Piura, Ucayali, Loreto each report four deaths, with Amazonas and Junín two, and Cusco and Lima one each. Three of the five regions with the largest increases lie on the northern coast, a zone exposed to Niño Costero conditions, with health systems warning of medicine and supply shortages as transmission season intensifies.

article.articleHeadline: BHWs face threats as vaccine fears slow Cebu measles-rubella drive
article.articleSummary: Measles-rubella vaccination drive in Cebu City, Central Visayas, Philippines struggles as vaccine fears slow uptake and health workers face hostility. As of Aug 18, 2026, only 12% of the region’s target 630,214 children have been vaccinated, far from a 95% coverage goal to halt measles and rubella transmission. Barangay health workers (BHWs) act as social mobilizers, informing parents and locating children, but reports include doors slammed in faces and threats involving a bolo; one BHW was nearly bitten by a dog. Health authorities emphasize vaccine safety and quality, noting the vaccines are not unique to Cebu and are used similarly across LGUs and abroad. Refusals are linked to social media misinformation, with parents urged to consult doctors, nurses, and midwives rather than rely on social media for information to close transmission gaps.

article.articleHeadline: Baguio eyes mosquito bacteria to curb dengue
article.articleSummary: Baguio City is eyed as a pilot site for Wolbachia-based dengue control, after two investing companies expressed interest in using the city as a model before wider rollout in the Philippines. The approach uses Wolbachia bacteria injected into Aedes aegypti to block dengue virus replication; not insect-modified and not harmful to humans. In Australia, Wolbachia has been released for about 15 years, with dengue cases down 77% and hospitalizations down 86%. Baguio has recorded 543 dengue cases since January, part of a Cordillera-wide total of 4,436 cases from Jan 4 to Aug 8, with spikes every two to three years and a projected mid-August peak this year, tapering by mid-October. Tacloban City reports 272 dengue cases as of Aug 8, up 31% from last year, with 374 dengue patients admitted from outside the city. Public health measures include fogging and antidengue spraying; residents urged to eliminate standing water and seek early care.

article.articleHeadline: Central Lombok Regency Government conducts TB contact tracing after the discovery of 17 new cases.
article.articleSummary: Central Lombok Regency, Lombok Tengah, Nusa Tenggara Barat, Indonesia, conducts TB contact tracing after identifying 17 new cases. Over one week of screening, 17 new positive tuberculosis cases (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) were detected. Screening focuses on Praya Barat, Pujut, and Praya Barat Daya subdistricts, with expansion planned to all 12 districts of Lombok Tengah due to prior distribution and limited testing capacity. The government targets 3,712 new TB cases in 2026 and will continue screening through November 2026. Confirmed cases will receive six months of uninterrupted treatment; if a dose is missed, the regimen must be restarted. The effort aims for early detection to interrupt transmission chains and reduce TB mortality. TB is infectious but curable with regular medication.

article.articleHeadline: Corn Waste and Papaya Leaves Processed into Malaria-Carrying Mosquito Repellent
article.articleSummary: Eco-Repel Spray, a malaria-vector repellent based on corn silk (Zea mays L.) and papaya leaves (Carica papaya L.), was developed by Gorontalo State University (UNG) researchers in Indonesia to offer a natural alternative to synthetic repellents. Implemented through a Community-Based Participatory Approach in Botumoito Village, Boalemo Regency, Gorontalo, the project involved La Ode Aman, Dizky Ramadani Putri Papeo, and Yuniarty Antu. Corn silk provides bioactive flavonoids, saponins, tannins, and essential oils that may disrupt mosquito host-seeking, with norbergenin potentially affecting malaria parasite growth. Papaya leaves add alkaloids, saponins, flavonoids, and phenolics, whose flavonoids contribute repellent effects. The formulation is combined with citronella oil (geraniol, citronellal) to extend protection. Household-friendly preparation: boil 50–100 g corn silk with 10–15 fresh papaya leaves in 1 L water for 20–30 minutes, filter, then mix 100 mL 70% ethanol with 1 mL citronella oil.

article.articleHeadline: There are 21 animal bite cases in the first half of 2026, Yogyakarta City is confirmed to remain rabies-free.
article.articleSummary: Yogyakarta City, Indonesia, remains rabies-free since 1997, with 21 animal-bite cases in the first half of 2026 but no rabies confirmed (all tests negative). Most bites involve domestic cats and dogs, including some incidents among owners. High vaccination coverage underpins the zero-rabies status: in 2025, 3,011 animals were vaccinated (2,435 cats, 565 dogs, 11 monkeys) across 14 subdistricts (kemantren). Vaccination services continued January–June 2026 at the City Veterinary Clinic. For exposure management, bites should be reported to the Department of Agriculture and Food (DPP); the wound should be washed with running water and soap for 10–15 minutes and the person taken to the nearest Puskesmas for follow-up. The biting animal undergoes a 14-day observation period per rabies incubation, to assess infection risk.

article.articleHeadline: MBG's Lab Tests in Bontang Find E. coli in Shredded Chicken.
article.articleSummary: Escherichia coli contamination was detected in shredded chicken (ayam suwir kemangi) served to students at Yayasan Vidatra in Bontang, according to laboratory tests by Dinas Kesehatan Kota Bontang. The sample originated from Dapur Satuan Pelayanan Pemenuhan Gizi Bontang Selatan 5 and was delivered on Monday, 10 August 2026. Of four tested items—nasi uduk, ayam suwir kemangi, tahu goreng, tumis wortel—E. coli was found only in the chicken dish. Dinkes notes the finding signals hygiene and sanitation gaps in processing and can trigger diarrhea and food poisoning. Authorities will coordinate with Dinas Ketahanan Pangan, Pertanian, dan Perikanan (DKP3) Bontang to evaluate the frozen chicken used by SPPG. Inspections flagged cross-contamination risks, including cooling and portioning in the same room, use of raw basil, and water quality for washing vegetables. The long gap—up to 10 hours—between cooking and serving is suspected as a major factor; a final conclusion on causality has not been reached.

article.articleHeadline: Pacet Sanatorium and the Tuberculosis Outbreak in the Dutch East Indies
article.articleSummary: On 6 September 1919, Pacet Sanatorium opened in Patjet, Priangan, billed as the Eerste sanatorium voor longlijders in Nederlandsch Oost-Indië. Built for about 45,000 guilders, it aimed to serve Europeans, Indo, and indigenous residents, but initial demand—roughly 50 requests—exceeded beds, prompting plans for wards for those who could not pay. Tuberculosis was already a major problem in the Indies: 1913 mortality in Batavia reached 18/10,000; Semarang 20/10,000; Surabaya 23/10,000. The 1928–1929 Staten-Generaal report described TB as very widespread, with urban data undercounts; Minahasa reportedly had around 40,000 cases. Pacet was built by Centrale Vereeniging tot Bestrijding der Tuberculose in Nederlandsch-Indië, with support from N. countess van Limburg Stirum-van Sminia, Queen Emma, and private donors; postwar government aid was limited. The sanatorium promoted open-air TB treatment, integrating living conditions, housing, and nutrition with care, amid debates over propaganda versus eradication.

article.articleHeadline: Sleman Health Office Reveals the Cause of Poisoning of 25 Elementary School Children in Prambanan
article.articleSummary: Escherichia coli-contaminated water used for cooking caused a food poisoning outbreak among 25 elementary students in Prambanan, Sleman Regency, Special Region of Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Laboratory tests showed E. coli at 105 CFU/mL in the cooking water and similar contamination on boiled green beans (kacang panjang). Investigators traced the likely source to the MBG (Makan Bergizi Gratis) master menu distributed to several schools on August 3, 2026, with symptoms appearing on August 4, consistent with the incubation period. Three students required hospitalization; the remainder were treated by local health teams and epidemiological tracing is ongoing. In response, the Sleman Health Office recommended immediate chlorination disinfection of the water supply and verification that all drinking water meets health standards. A formal review of MBG kitchen providers will be conducted in an internal satgas meeting.

article.articleHeadline: Can Animal Scabies Be Transmitted to Humans? Medical Facts and How to Prevent It.
article.articleSummary: Scabies can be transmitted from pets to humans (a zoonosis) through close contact with dogs or cats infested by Sarcoptes scabiei. The canine mite (Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis) differs from the human mite (var. hominis) and cannot complete its life cycle on human skin; infections are self-limiting and typically resolve within a few days to two weeks after contact ends. Symptoms in people include intense itching, small red bumps, and a warm rash at areas of direct contact; unlike typical human scabies, lesions can appear anywhere touched. If itching persists or involves spaces like between the fingers, consult a dermatologist to exclude human-to-human scabies. Treatment targets both hosts: treat the pet with antiparasitic injections, spot-on products, or medicated shampoo, and use topical permethrin or antihistamines for humans. Clean bedding and vacuum the home to remove mites and prevent reinfection.

article.articleHeadline: Detecting Hepatitis B Among Pregnant Women: A Growing Concern at Ho Teaching Hospital
article.articleSummary: As of 18 August 2026, Ho Teaching Hospital in Ho, Ghana, is conducting an ongoing study to detect Hepatitis B (HBV) among pregnant women at antenatal visits, using rapid HBsAg testing to enable early diagnosis and reduce mother‑to‑child transmission. The undergraduate project by Biochemistry and Molecular Biology students at the University of Health and Allied Sciences (UHAS) aims to enroll 300 pregnant women; preliminary data from the first 90 participants show 13 positives and 77 negatives, not representing the full cohort. Recruitment was expanded to Ho Municipal Hospital to boost sample size. Challenges include lower-than-expected antenatal attendance and scheduling conflicts with lectures. Positive cases may undergo confirmatory testing. The study highlights the importance of continued screening, awareness, and timely follow‑up to protect mothers and newborns.
